title: Boundary of Binary Tree
prompt:
The boundary of a binary tree is the concatenation of the root, the left boundary, the leaves ordered from left to right, and the reverse of the right boundary, in that order.

The left boundary is defined as the set of nodes on the path from the root to the leftmost leaf, excluding leaves and the root (the leftmost leaf is found by always preferring the left child, falling back to the right child only when there is no left child). Similarly, the right boundary is the set of nodes on the path from the root to the rightmost leaf, excluding leaves and the root, and this boundary is reversed before being added to the final answer.

Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the values of its boundary as a list, with no value duplicated (a node that is both part of a boundary path and a leaf is only counted once, as a leaf). The tree is given as a level-order array where `null` marks a missing child (the standard LeetCode serialization). Your function receives this array directly; the starter code includes a helper that builds the tree from it.

examples.explanation: Root is 1. There's no left boundary (root has no left child). Leaves left-to-right are 3 and 4. The right boundary is just node 2, which is also the rightmost path but 2 turns out to be a leaf's ancestor here so it's included reversed: [2].
Root 1, left boundary node 2, leaves left-to-right (4,5,8,9,7), right boundary node 3 (reversed, but it's a single node here).
A tree with only a root node has no left/right boundary and the root itself is the only leaf, so the boundary is just [1].

constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4]
hints: Break the problem into three independent pieces computed separately, then concatenated: the left boundary (excluding leaves), the leaves (left to right), and the right boundary (excluding leaves, added in reverse).

For the left boundary, walk down always preferring the left child (falling to the right child only if there's no left child), stopping before including any node that turns out to be a leaf. Do the mirror image for the right boundary.

Collect leaves with a straightforward DFS that checks for 'no left and no right child', visiting left before right so the leaf order is naturally left-to-right; be careful the root itself is only added once (as the very first element), even if the root itself has no children (i.e., is a leaf) or is part of what would otherwise be a boundary path.

solution.approach: Split the boundary into three parts computed independently and then joined: (1) the left boundary — walk down from the root's left child, always preferring to go left and only going right when there's no left child, stopping (not including) once a leaf is reached; (2) all leaves collected via DFS in left-to-right order; (3) the right boundary computed the mirror way from the root's right child, then reversed. The root is added once at the very start (unless the tree is just a single node, since that lone node is fully captured as 'the only leaf'). Special-case a tree with only a root: return just [root.val].
solution.spaceComplexity: O(h), h = tree height, excluding output
